title: Recording business, royalties, and Flat Foot Floogie
summary: Stewart says recordings were not much of a rip-off in his time and that royalties on Flat Foot Floogie were his best; Crouch sees it anticipating Louis Jordan.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: In those days, how did the guys look at the recording industry? Did they consider -- I mean, today, most jazz musicians consider just recording industry as just a huge rip-off. Did guys feel the same way in those years?

Well, I don't think it could be compared to nowadays, you know, the rip-off department and what have you. They weren't too bad, what I mean, I might say. I was well paid for my recording, my -- even with my groups and what have you.
Royalties are great, especially on the tunes that I was connected with, you know, especially the 'Flatfoot Floogie.' That was my top tune.
*Native of Indonesia (Dutch East Indies) where he edited a magazine, Swing, during 1937-38 before emigrating to England, then America, 1939.

Yeah, we were saying about "Flatfoot Floogie" that "Flatfoot Floogie" may have been kind of a predictor of some of the things Louie Jordan did, some of the things that eventually evolved into rhythm and blues.
Because you have a kind of a simple kind of a line that has a certain kind of a rhythm.
Right. I would imagine that Louie Jordan, besides the popularity of it --

You know, if you do something that's popular, people tend to emulate it because they recognize something that people like. And so you -- that was -- that particular recording has done you well, in terms of --
